claims.source: Wikipedia biography; Johns Hopkins Sheridan Libraries page

claims.claim: She settled in Chicago in 1919 per the Smithsonian; Wikipedia says she came to Chicago in 1927.
claims.uncertainty: prefer the Smithsonian finding aid, but the conflict is unresolved.

claims.claim: Hired by Dorsey in the late 1920s to sing in a trio introducing his songs to Chicago-area Black churches, she became his business partner: marketing his songs, organizing his finances, developing new markets, and helping launch the Dorsey House of Music (1932) and the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses.

claims.source: Johns Hopkins Sheridan Libraries page; Wikipedia

claims.claim: She formed the Sallie Martin Singers in 1940 after a dispute with Dorsey; the group featured her daughter Cora Martin-Moore, Dinah Washington (then Ruth Jones), and Brother Joe May.
claims.uncertainty: notable for launching a major secular star (Washington) from gospel infrastructure.

claims.claim: The Sallie Martin Singers are described as the first all-woman gospel group.
claims.uncertainty: significant if true; "first" claims need dedicated verification.

claims.claim: In 1940 she co-founded the Martin and Morris Music Company with Kenneth Morris.
claims.uncertainty: see Martin and Morris entity.

claims.claim: She retired from touring with the Sallie Martin Singers in the mid-1950s; the group continued for decades.
claims.uncertainty: suggests working-class touring strain as a factor.

claims.claim: Morris (1917–1989), born in New York, began as a professional jazz musician, studied at the Manhattan Conservatory of Music, and relocated permanently to Chicago after falling ill while performing at the 1934 Chicago World's Fair.
claims.uncertainty: migration-via-music-work story parallels the Great Migration.

claims.claim: He spent six years with the Lillian Bowles Music House before partnering with Sallie Martin.
claims.uncertainty: documents another woman — Bowles — as a gospel publishing employer.

claims.claim: He was one of the first musicians to introduce the Hammond organ to gospel music.
claims.uncertainty: qualified "one of the first"; the exact priority claim is contested territory.

claims.claim: He introduced the Hammond organ to the gospel recording industry by accompanying Mahalia Jackson on the 1947 recording of "Move On Up a Little Higher."
claims.uncertainty: a more precise, recording-specific claim; needs discographic confirmation.

claims.claim: In 1940 he arranged and published the well-known version of "Just a Closer Walk with Thee."
claims.uncertainty: consistent with Hymnology Archive account.

claims.claim: Rev. Cobbs privately funded the printing of one of Morris's first songs, "Heaven Bells," in 1937, distributed through First Church of Deliverance.
claims.uncertainty: shows church-based financing of gospel publishing.

claims.claim: Kenneth Morris and Sallie Martin co-owned the nation's oldest continuously running Black gospel music publishing company, established in Chicago in 1940 and operating into the 1980s.
claims.uncertainty: "oldest continuously running" is the archive's characterization; collection includes correspondence 1941–1980 and business/financial records 1940–1978.

claims.claim: Martin spent most of her time on the road with her singers promoting the firm's compositions; Morris stayed in Chicago arranging, composing, and notating music; Morris's wife Necie handled most of the company's paperwork.
claims.uncertainty: a clear gendered division of touring labor vs. back-office/creative labor, all within Black ownership.

James Cleveland; historian Clarence Boyer called it "the only publishing house to solicit and publish songs of most of the established and new composers during gospel music's golden age, 1945–1965."
claims.uncertainty: the Boyer quotation is strong if accurately quoted; needs the original Boyer text.

claims.claim: The firm acquired Lillian Bowles's catalog in 1959 and the catalogs of Roberta Martin and Theodore Frye around 1978; Sallie Martin sold her interest in 1973; Morris's widow Necie Seaberry Morris ran the business until 1993.
claims.uncertainty: catalog acquisitions show consolidation of Black gospel publishing under Black ownership.

claims.source: Los Angeles Sentinel; Johns Hopkins Sheridan Libraries page

claims.source: City of Chicago, Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events (Maxwell Street Market history)

claims.uncertainty: the city's own account centers a collective, technological, commercial ecosystem — not a single inventor.

claims.claim: The market was moved in 1994 for University of Illinois Chicago expansion and moved again in fall 2008.
claims.uncertainty: displacement by institutional development is part of the infrastructure story.

claims.claim: Black Southern workers and performers animated the market in the 1940s; the district's destruction was tied to expressway and UIC development.
claims.uncertainty: museum education department source.

claims.uncertainty: consistent across enthusiast and oral-history sources; discographic scholarship needed for firm verification.

claims.uncertainty: a key Chicago blues discographic claim; verify against discographies.

claims.uncertainty: the independent-local-label-to-national-label path is the key infrastructure finding.

claims.claim: A Chicago producer whose dark, mechanical Midwest funk shaped Do or Die's *Picture This*; the album's success introduced him as a behind-the-boards architect of the Chicago sound.
claims.uncertainty: producer-as-infrastructure; needs interview or profile sourcing.

claims.claim: An R&B vocalist and frequent collaborator on the mid-1990s Chicago rap records (notably "Po Pimp").
claims.uncertainty: singer infrastructure bridging R&B and rap; biographical details not researched in this pass.

claims.claim: An up-and-coming independent Chicago label that first released Do or Die's "Po Pimp," generating the local hit that drew Rap-A-Lot's attention; the *Picture This* sessions were partly recorded at Creator's Way Studios in Chicago.
claims.uncertainty: exactly the kind of small local imprint this track is meant to surface; needs primary business or discographic confirmation.

claims.claim: A contemporary November 1986 SPIN feature described it as Chicago's dance-specialist shop, serving mostly DJs with 12-inches, Philly soul, and imports.

claims.claim: The Hyde Park location strongly supported independent soul and hip-hop.
claims.uncertainty: genre/community role from a single source.

claims.claim: The store opened in 2010 at 1377 E. 53rd Street, becoming a South Side neighborhood record store after Dr. Wax's closure, specializing in rare dance mixes, jazz, soul, and disco.
claims.uncertainty: succession story (Dr. Wax → Hyde Park Records) is the key point; founding-ownership details unresolved.

claims.claim: Ownership changed in 2012 and the store continued serving the community and visitors.
claims.uncertainty: thin source; current operating status not re-verified.

claims.claim: Bob Koester moved to Chicago in 1958, took over Seymour's Jazz Mart at 439 S. Wabash in 1959, and renamed it the Jazz Record Mart.
claims.uncertainty: the label's own history; corroborated by JazzTimes.

claims.claim: Delmark Records operated beneath the store, documenting local blues and jazz; the label released Roscoe Mitchell's *Sound* in 1966 and maintained long ties to AACM recordings.
claims.uncertainty: store-as-label-incubator; AACM connection is significant for the Black avant-garde.

claims.claim: The Jazz Record Mart brand dated to 1962; the store ran 5,000 square feet; Koester valued daily contact with customers.

claims.source: Chicago Tribune (via Jazz Promo Services reprint)

claims.claim: Founder of Delmark Records and the Jazz Record Mart; celebrated in a 2021 Delmark retrospective on his life and legacy; died at 88.
claims.uncertainty: the white-owner-in-Black-music-retail dynamic deserves explicit, careful handling in flagship copy; not analyzed here.

claims.claim: Rose Records was a family-owned Chicago record business and "a Chicago institution for over 60 years"; James L. "Jim" Rosenbloom (d. 2021, age 80) was its President and Co-Owner, and the son of founder Aaron Rosenbloom.
claims.uncertainty: confirms family ownership, the founder's name (Aaron), and 60+ year duration (founding no later than ~1961).

claims.claim: The chain is described as founded in 1931 as Rose Radio by Aaron Rosenbloom, growing to 35 stores with a three-story Wabash flagship carrying 100,000 titles, and closing in 1995.
claims.uncertainty: inadequate sourcing — merch copy, not journalism or archives; every element (1931, 35 stores, flagship, 1995) needs Tribune reporting, city directories, or advertisements.

claims.claim: Rose Records is cited as the Chicago example of a local/regional record-store chain in a peer-reviewed study of record stores in majority-Black neighborhoods in Chicago, Milwaukee, and Detroit, 1970–2010.
claims.uncertainty: scholarly classification; the article's broader finding — record stores were once more clustered in predominantly Black areas than today, and 1980–1990 failure rates were higher outside majority-white areas — frames the whole retail-infrastructure story.
